passages.where: A sleepless singer lies awake musing and pondering, and the same questions go round: will the Lord spurn us forever, has his promise failed, has God forgotten to be gracious? The site's plain note says the psalm does not pretend that thinking about God always helps; at first remembering only brought groans. It also says he did not stop asking. He kept talking to God through the night.

Then the psalm turns. The singer resolves to remember the works of the LORD and ponder his mighty deeds, and he recalls the exodus. The site's plain note says he did not find comfort by thinking about his feelings, but by turning to what God had done. The mind does not go quiet by being emptied; it is given something truer to dwell on.

David marvels that the LORD knows him completely: his sitting and rising, his thoughts from afar, his words before he speaks. The site's plain note says the psalm holds both fear and comfort: God knows the worst about you, and he has not let go. The thoughts that circle all night are not hidden from him, and they do not surprise him.

Paul tells the church to think on whatever is true, honorable, right, pure, lovely and admirable. The site's plain note says he gives a practice, not a switch, and that the passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder or depression, which need care, not blame. It asks what the mind dwells on most of the day, and whether it is true.

In the dry wilderness of Judah, David thinks of God through the watches of the night. The site's plain note offers a way to use the waking hours: not to force sleep, and not to worry, but to remember what God has done and where his hand has held you. It adds that even when your grip on God feels weak, his grip on you is not.

A father urges his son to trust the LORD with all his heart rather than lean on his own understanding, and promises that God will make his paths straight. The site's note on the chapter sets it among the father's teaching to trust the LORD rather than his own understanding. Thinking hard is not forbidden; leaning the whole weight of a life on one's own analysis is.

Judah sings of a strong city where the LORD keeps in perfect peace those who trust him, as the site's note on the chapter puts it. The peace belongs to the mind that is steadfast because it trusts, not to the mind that has finally solved every question. It is something God keeps, not something the mind manufactures.

James tells anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault. The site's note sets this beside his teaching on trials, rich and poor, and temptation. A person stuck going over and over a decision can stop and ask, and God does not scold them for needing to.

The Teacher says to be joyful in the day of prosperity and, in the day of adversity, to consider that God has made both, so that no one can discover what will come after. The site's note on the chapter says the Teacher tried to be wise and found wisdom beyond reach. Some questions will not yield to more thinking, and admitting that is itself a kind of wisdom.

In a parable found only in Mark, a man scatters seed and then sleeps and rises while it grows, though he does not know how. The site's note says the point falls not on the man's effort but on the growth that happens without him, and the plain note asks where we are trying to force growth that only God can give. Much of God's work happens while we are not watching, and not thinking.

misread.taken: Take captive every thought is often given to people troubled by unwanted, repeating thoughts as an instruction: try harder, push the thought out, and treat its return as a sign of weak faith.
misread.says: The site's plain note says the verse is about Paul's dealing with rival teaching in Corinth, bringing the church's thinking back under Christ; it is not a technique for pushing unwanted thoughts out of your mind. To anyone troubled by thoughts that come again and again, it says gently that having such a thought is not the same as choosing it, and it is not sin, that trying harder to capture it often makes it louder, and that this can be part of anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder and can be treated.

whole: Overthinking is usually invisible to everyone but the person doing it. They replay a conversation from Tuesday and rewrite what they should have said. They run every possible outcome of a decision until they cannot make it. They read a short reply to a message and spend an evening deciding what it meant. At night the mind speeds up rather than slowing down, and the same questions come round again. It can look like conscientiousness, and sometimes it began that way. But it is tiring, it rarely produces a better answer, and it often leaves a person more anxious than when they started. For some it is part of anxiety, depression or obsessive thoughts that need a doctor's care, and that is not a failure of faith.

Scripture knows this kind of night. A temple singer in Psalm 77 lay awake with his spirit pondering, asking whether God had forgotten to be gracious, and at first remembering God only made him groan. The Teacher in Ecclesiastes tried to think his way to the bottom of life and found wisdom beyond reach. Underneath much overthinking is something the Bible would recognize: the hope that if we can only think it through far enough we can make ourselves safe, avoid every mistake, and control what will happen. Proverbs calls that leaning on your own understanding. It is a very human thing to do, and most of us do it about whatever we fear losing.

So the Bible's wisdom is not to stop thinking, but to change what the mind rests on. The singer of Psalm 77 turned from his own questions to remembering what God had done, and Paul tells the church to think on what is true and good. When the mind is going round at night, David's way is to remember God through the watches of the night rather than to force sleep. When a decision will not settle, James says to ask God, who gives without finding fault, and then to act on the light you have. It helps to say the worry aloud to God, or to a friend, rather than letting it circle in silence. And when thoughts keep returning that you do not want, the site's note on 2 Corinthians 10 says plainly that having them is not sinning, and that a doctor or a counsellor can help.

The hope Scripture gives is that you are known more completely than you can know yourself, and held by someone who does not need you to figure everything out. The LORD understands your thoughts from afar, and he keeps in perfect peace the mind that trusts him. The seed grows while the farmer sleeps, though he does not know how. Some questions will stay open, and some nights will still be long. But the one who holds tomorrow is awake when you are not, and you are allowed to lie down and sleep in peace.
sit: What is the question your mind keeps going back to, and what would it mean to hand it to God tonight and leave it with him until morning?

prayer.lead: A prayer for lying down at night. The site's plain note suggests praying verse 8 slowly, more than once, when sleep will not come, and says that if sleeplessness goes on for weeks it is wise to see a doctor.

next.label: Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?

careLines.text: Having such a thought is not the same as choosing it, and it is not sin.
A doctor or a counsellor can help, and a pastor or a friend you trust can stand with you.
Lost sleep and heavy thoughts are worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a failure of faith.
